tldr: PushMimic is a reinforcement learning framework that adapts humanoid box pushing postures in real time to box mass and ramp inclination without directly measuring them, starting from just a single level-ground kinematic motion via sampling-based trajectory optimization and reference distillation.
hero_caption: Overall framework of PushMimic. Left: a level-ground reference motion is dynamically augmented. Center: the dataset is distilled into a single policy that observes only the level-ground reference motion while tracking augmented motions. Right: the policy autonomously adapts to unknown environments.
overview:
Having a humanoid robot push a large box becomes difficult on real-world floors where box mass and ground inclination are unknown beforehand. For heavy boxes or steep ramps, the robot must lean forward deeply and brace its feet like a human does, or the pushing reaction force will topple it backward. However, capturing human motion for every combination of slope and weight is impractical.

To address this, the authors asked: wouldn't a single reference motion of pushing a light box on level ground be enough? First, using sampling-based trajectory optimization (SBTO) informed by a quasi-static model, they automatically generate a dynamically feasible motion dataset covering various masses and slopes. Second—and this is the key insight—they decouple observation and reward during reinforcement learning: the policy is shown only the "level-ground reference motion", while the reward evaluates tracking against the "true optimal motion for that environment".

As a result, without ever being told the mass or inclination, the robot senses the pushing reaction force from the box and autonomously adjusts its posture, realizing "it's heavy right now, so I should lean forward". In simulation on the Unitree G1, the success rate increased significantly and the load on the arms decreased. Furthermore, in physical treadmill experiments, the robot demonstrated adaptive capabilities by smoothly deepening its forward lean without falling over, even when weights were added mid-push or the ramp steepened.
contributions: Proposed PushMimic, an adaptive humanoid box pushing framework that performs automatic dynamic motion augmentation and one-stage policy distillation from a single level-ground kinematic motion.
Raised the success rate from 57.8% to 88.8% and reduced the arm cost of push by 22% compared to a baseline in simulation across box masses from 5 to 15 kg and ramp inclinations up to 15°.

Demonstrated zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, showing that it can immediately adapt torso pitch during continuous pushing as box mass (up to 19 kg) and ramp inclination (up to 12.6°) change.

sections.heading: How to adapt to heavy boxes and steep slopes from just one level-ground motion
sections.summary: Humanoid box pushing is difficult because appropriate pushing postures change with contact forces. Existing work either produced unnatural postures through reward engineering or was limited to tracking motions fixed to recording conditions. This work develops an approach that adapts to unknown mass and inclination from a single level-ground motion.
sections.details:
Demand is rising for humanoids to transport goods in manufacturing and logistics, but pushing large boxes is not easy. Physical parameters of the task—such as box mass, friction, and floor inclination—are not known beforehand and change with every push.

For example, when pushing a heavy box on a ramp, humans naturally pitch their torso forward deeply and shift their foot positions backward to brace themselves. If a robot tries to push with brute force while maintaining an upright posture suited for level ground, it not only wastes energy but also falls backward due to the reaction force, failing the task.

Existing reinforcement learning approaches generally fall into two camps. One trains policies purely with task rewards, but this leaves which body parts push and how undefined, often resulting in unnatural pushing styles and tedious reward tuning. The other tracks human reference motions like motion capture, but available human motion data is mostly on level ground. Recording motions for every combination of mass and inclination is impossible.

To solve this, the authors propose "PushMimic". Starting from just one reference motion recorded on level ground, it uses dynamics-aware optimization to automatically generate motion data for diverse environments, distilling them into a single policy that can infer the situation from its own state and adapt its posture even in unknown environments.

captions.F1: The physical G1 humanoid pushing a box on a 10° inclined treadmill. As weights are added mid-push—increasing box mass from 10 kg to 15 kg, then 19 kg—the robot automatically deepens its torso pitch angle to adapt.

sections.heading: Mass-producing load-resistant motions with physics models and trajectory optimization
sections.summary: Based on a simplified quasi-static mechanics model of human box pushing, the authors derived that torso forward lean and foot backward placement are essential. By incorporating these as a prior and a deadzone into sampling-based trajectory optimization, physically plausible reference motions across various conditions are generated all at once.
sections.details:
### II-A & II-B Posture Intuition from a Simplified Model
The authors first formulated box pushing on a slope as a 2D planar quasi-static model (Fig. 3). When the reaction force of the box pushing force $F=mg(\sin\alpha+\mu\cos\alpha)$ acts on the hands, it produces a moment that tends to tip the robot downslope. Solving the moment balance about the center of pressure (CoP: the support pivot under the foot) reveals that the required forward lean angle $\psi$ of the center of mass is the sum of the lean required to stand against gravity and an additional lean to resist the pushing force (which scales with inclination angle $\alpha$ and box mass $m$). Because the pivot can only exist within the foot support polygon, balancing mechanically requires the robot to "pitch its torso forward" and "pull its feet downslope".

### II-C & II-D Dynamics-Aware Trajectory Optimization (SBTO)
Leveraging this insight, sampling-based trajectory optimization (SBTO) generates reference motions that do not collapse in a physics simulator across a grid of 176 combinations of box mass (5 to 15 kg) and ramp inclination (0 to 15°). SBTO does not explicitly formulate intermittent foot and hand contacts, but instead searches through parallel simulator rollouts, yielding robust solutions.

The cost function for optimization includes several design choices:
- **Torso pitch prior**: Mimicking the relationship in equation (1), an offset is applied to pitch the torso forward as inclination steepens and the box becomes heavier, smoothly guiding the posture from the level-ground reference toward a forward lean.
- **Foot placement deadzone**: Strictly tracking the level-ground foot positions prevents feet from stepping backward, causing the box to stall on steep ramps. Therefore, a wide deadzone is provided along the slope direction, allowing feet to freely place backward according to dynamics within that range. This preserves the original contact timing while providing the necessary bracing support.

captions.F3: Planar quasi-static model of the box pushing task. It illustrates the mechanical relationship showing that to maintain balance against the pushing reaction force F, the CoM (center of mass) must lean forward relative to the CoP (center of pressure) and the feet must be placed backward.

sections.heading: A distillation technique that elicits adaptability by showing only level-ground motion
sections.summary: By feeding the policy only level-ground reference motion information while using environment-matched augmented motions for reinforcement learning rewards, the authors decoupled observation and reward. This lets the robot autonomously infer the environment from contact feedback and adopt the optimal forward lean.
sections.details:
### III-A Markov Decision Process (MDP) Design
The generated dataset of 176 motions is distilled into a single neural network policy that runs on the physical robot. Each parallel environment is assigned a different mass and inclination $\theta=(m, \alpha)$, but the crucial feature is that the reference motions used in observations and rewards are decoupled.

- **Observation (policy input)**: Robot joint states, angular velocities, gravity vector in the base frame, and relative box pose/velocity, along with the nominal level-ground reference joint positions and velocities. True values of box mass and ramp inclination are not provided at all.
- **Reward (evaluation metric)**: Rewards are based on tracking errors against the "augmented reference motion" corresponding to the true task parameters of that environment. In addition, contacts between the box and body parts other than the feet and hands immediately terminate the episode, preventing cheating such as pushing with knees or shoulders.

### III-B One-Stage Distillation via Decoupled Observation and Reward
Why does this method allow adaptation? The answer lies in the pushing feedback (reaction forces) felt from the box. With a heavy box or steep slope, pushing with the same effort does not accelerate the box as quickly, and the direction of the gravity vector on the base changes. In seeking high rewards (the posture of the augmented motion), the policy naturally discerns environmental differences from the history of observable feedback and learns to lean forward without being explicitly told to do so.

Unlike two-stage approaches that train separate policies for individual environments before distilling them, this method uses asymmetric Actor-Critic from the start (giving privileged true task parameters and augmented motions only to the Critic), successfully condensing everything into a single policy in just one reinforcement learning stage.

sections.heading: Leaping to an 88.8% success rate and remarkable endurance on a real treadmill
sections.summary: In simulation, PushMimic achieved an 88.8% success rate compared to 57.8% for the baseline, reducing arm joint load by 22%. On the physical Unitree G1 humanoid, it demonstrated real-time posture adaptation by pitching its torso to keep pushing even when mass increased from 10 kg to 19 kg or inclination reached 12.6° mid-push.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Experimental Setup and Validation of Augmented Motions
Experiments were conducted using the Unitree G1, a compact humanoid standing about 1.3 m tall. Flat plates with passive damping hinges were mounted to the hands to maintain surface contact with the box (Fig. 4).
Evaluating the generated augmented motion data showed that as inclination angle and mass increased, average torso pitch angle deepened smoothly, increasing from 43.6° at 5 kg to 59.3° at 15 kg on a 15° slope (Fig. 7). This confirms that motions matching the predictions of the simplified mechanics model were automatically generated.

### IV-C Simulation Comparisons
PushMimic was compared against a Vanilla baseline that simply tilted the level-ground motion to match the slope.
- **Task Completion (Success Rate)**: Across the entire grid, the Vanilla baseline achieved only 57.8%, while the proposed method reached a dominant 88.8% (Fig. 8). PushMimic reliably pushed the box through high-mass (11 kg and above) and steep-slope regimes where Vanilla stalled or tipped over. The 50% success force ($F_{50}$) also improved significantly from 66 N to 92 N.
- **Adaptiveness**: PushMimic scored an adaptiveness of 0.99 for inclination and 0.83 for mass (compared to 0.28 and -0.20 for Vanilla), nearly perfectly reproducing posture changes from the augmented motions. Even when parameters changed abruptly mid-push, the policy smoothly adapted its posture in real time (Fig. 5).
- **Cost of Push**: Based on the sum of squared joint torques in the arms during successful trials, the proposed method reduced pushing cost by 22%. Instead of bracing purely with arm strength, the robot pushes efficiently by leveraging the falling weight of its tilted torso.

### IV-D Real-Robot Treadmill Experiments
A variable-incline treadmill was used as an endless ramp for physical robot validation. A 1.52-second gait cycle (advancing 0.94 m) was looped with the belt running at 0.6 m/s, allowing continuous pushing in place.
1. **Online Mass Variation**: While pushing on a 10° incline, weights were manually placed on the box to increase mass from 10 kg to 15 kg to 19 kg. Torso pitch immediately deepened from 46.8° to 48.4° to 52.8° (Fig. 1).
2. **Online Inclination Variation**: Pushing a 10 kg box, the treadmill was tilted from 0° to 12.6° over 46 seconds. Torso pitch smoothly deepened from 39.1° to 48.3° at a rate of 0.71° per degree of slope.
Across 9 runs totaling 8.5 minutes and 307 m of walking, the robot maintained stable box pushing without a single fall.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Work
sections.summary: PushMimic generates a dynamically feasible motion set from a single level-ground motion, achieving robust box pushing that adapts to unobserved environmental parameters by decoupling observation and reward. Overcoming grid search compute costs and reliance on external MoCap are key next steps.
sections.details:
This paper presented PushMimic, a humanoid box pushing control framework that adapts to unknown box mass and floor inclination starting from a single level-ground kinematic reference motion.

By combining dynamics-aware trajectory optimization for motion augmentation with a one-stage policy distillation that feeds level-ground motion into observations and augmented motion into rewards, the robot autonomously adapts its forward lean using only the contact feedback it feels. In addition to major gains in success rate and energy efficiency in simulation, its effectiveness was demonstrated under harsh load variation tests on a physical Unitree G1 treadmill setup.

The authors note two main limitations. First, because task parameters are discretized across a grid to generate motions, computational cost scales exponentially as parameter dimensions increase. Future work should explore sampling-based augmentation rather than exhaustive grid search. Second, the physical experiments relied on an external motion capture system to track box pose. For autonomous operation in real logistics environments or on outdoor ramps, onboard sensing using cameras or LiDAR will be required.

takeaways: Decoupling the reference motions used in observations and rewards allows the robot to implicitly infer context from physical contact feedback and adapt its motion without explicit task parameter estimation modules.
Because kinematic retargeting cannot produce contact-aware posture adaptations (such as leaning forward or bracing feet), simulator-in-the-loop dynamic augmentation (SBTO) is essential.

Using physical models to identify which degrees of freedom to loosen (such as torso pitch priors and foot placement deadzones) and embedding them into optimization costs is an effective, practical design strategy.
limitations: Generating reference motions via an exhaustive grid search over task parameters (mass and inclination) faces exponential computational scaling if more parameters, such as box dimensions or friction coefficients, are added.
Tracking the box pose on the physical robot currently requires an external motion capture system, meaning full autonomy via onboard cameras or tactile sensors alone has not yet been achieved.
